concerns.concern_text: The two acceptance criteria (p50? p99? p999? latency under 200ms, and 5000 RPS sustained for how long, under what load shape?) are stated without specifying percentile targets for latency, load profile duration, or test harness methodology. As written they are ambiguous and cannot be reliably pass/fail tested at an acceptance stage.

There is no business-level success metric anywhere in the design doc — no target fraud catch rate, false-positive rate, dollar value saved, or detection precision/recall target. Latency and throughput are operational targets, not success metrics for a fraud scoring product.

The design explicitly describes logging full card numbers and customer names to CloudWatch for debugging purposes. No redaction or masking layer is described. This is a blocking defect: raw PAN data in logs is a PCI DSS violation and an unacceptable PII exposure risk.

The CloudWatch log group that receives card numbers and customer names has no defined retention policy. Without a retention cap, sensitive data persists indefinitely. This is called out explicitly in the data flow diagram.

The service processes card transaction data (including full card numbers). There is no mention of a PCI DSS scope assessment, cardholder data environment (CDE) boundary definition, or any compensating controls. This must be resolved before the design is approved.

The design document contains no rollback procedure. For a real-time fraud scoring service sitting in a payment critical path, a failed deployment without a documented rollback plan carries significant operational and financial risk.

The data flow diagram shows a single fraud scoring service node with no mention of redundancy, multi-AZ deployment, or failover strategy. At 5000 RPS on a critical payment path, any single-node failure is a full service outage.

No circuit breaker or fallback behavior is described for the fraud scoring service. If the service degrades (e.g., model backend slow), callers have no documented degraded-mode behavior — accept-all, reject-all, or cached score.

There is no infrastructure cost estimate in the design doc for the compute required to sustain 5000 RPS, CloudWatch ingestion costs (which will be high given verbose PII-laden logs), or any autoscaling ceiling. This is required at design gate.
No autoscaling maximum or compute cap is defined. With 5000 RPS sustained throughput targets and no cap, runaway scaling events could result in unbounded cost exposure.

agent_responses.reasoning: This design has two blocking defects that prevent approval: (1) full PAN (card numbers) and customer names are being written to CloudWatch logs with no redaction — an explicit PCI DSS violation and severe PII exposure — and (2) the service processes card transaction data with zero mention of a PCI scope assessment or CDE boundary, which is a mandatory pre-condition for any card-data-touching service. Beyond the blockers, the design is materially incomplete from a PM perspective: there are no business-level success metrics (only latency/throughput operational targets), acceptance criteria lack percentile and duration specificity making them untestable, there is no rollback plan, no redundancy strategy, no circuit breaker fallback, and no cost estimate or ceiling. The data flow diagram confirms the PII-in-logs and missing retention policy issues. I am voting to block. The team must at minimum: strip or redact PII from logs, complete a PCI scope review, add a log retention policy, define measurable success metrics with testable criteria, and document rollback and failover strategies before returning to this gate.

agent_responses.reasoning: The design has two blocking issues that must be resolved before this gate can pass. First, full card PANs and customer names are intentionally written to CloudWatch logs with no redaction — this is both a PCI DSS violation and a serious PII exposure. Second, the service handles card transaction data with no PCI scope assessment documented anywhere in the design. Beyond the blockers, there are significant reliability gaps: no timeouts are specified on the synchronous 200ms SLA path, no circuit breaker or fallback is defined for the 5000 RPS critical path, and there is no backpressure strategy for burst traffic. Additionally, the CloudWatch log group has no retention policy (compounding the PII risk), there is no rollback plan for the release, and no autoscaling cost ceiling is defined. The combination of blocking compliance defects and multiple missing reliability patterns makes it impossible to approve this design as-is. The team should: (1) introduce PAN/PII masking before any log emission, (2) commission a PCI scope assessment, (3) add retention policy to the log group, (4) define per-call timeouts aligned to the 200ms budget, (5) add circuit breaker + fallback logic, (6) specify load-shedding/backpressure controls, (7) document rollback procedure, and (8) set autoscaling caps.

agent_responses.reasoning: Two blocking issues prevent gate approval. First, full PANs and customer names are written to CloudWatch logs without redaction — this is a direct PCI DSS (Requirement 3) violation and a GDPR/CCPA PII exposure. Second, the design handles card transactions with no PCI scope assessment on record, which is a prerequisite for any compliant build. Beyond the blockers, there are four additional high/medium concerns: (1) the CloudWatch log group has no retention policy, creating both regulatory and cost exposure; (2) autoscaling has no defined cost ceiling despite a 5,000 RPS target, leaving the spend envelope unbounded; (3) no cost estimate exists in the document at all; and (4) encryption at rest for the log group storing card data is unaddressed. The gate decision is BLOCK pending remediation of the two blocking items as a minimum, with the remaining concerns resolved or formally accepted before re-submission.
